attribution_note: Speaker is an unnamed wandering brahmana who keeps the ajagara (python) vow; 'Ajagara' names the vow, though Ganguli calls him 'the sage Ajagara'. He answers Prahlada, and the whole exchange is told by Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Rightful' renders dharmya (consistent with dharma); the qualifier matters: only lawful enjoyments are accepted.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a person can move through the world free of grief. Bhishma tells how Prahlada asked a serene, childlike wandering brahmana the secret of his contentment. The sage says beings arise and perish by their own nature, every union ends in parting, so he neither rejoices nor grieves; he feasts or fasts, sleeps in palaces or on bare ground, as things come. This verse states his rule, and Bhishma ends by saying whoever keeps this vow lives happily.

key_terms.sense: by chance, without one's own striving
an enjoyment that is lawful, in keeping with dharma
the python's vow: lying still and taking whatever comes

core_teaching: Contentment comes from neither rejecting what rightfully arrives nor straining after what is hard to get. The sage's peace rests on seeing that gain and loss come and go by their own course.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translator's notes (reporting Nilakantha)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli explains ajagara as the large snake that lies still and eats only what comes near. He notes Nilakantha reads the sage's 'causeless' origin of beings theistically, as Brahman, while Ganguli keeps the plain sense, possibly a religious indifferentism.

The Bhagavata retells Prahlada meeting a dust-covered sage near the Sahya hills who lives the python's way: no effort for gain, rich or poor food and bedding accepted as they come, python and bee as teachers.

practical_reading: Teachers use the ajagara ideal for non-grasping contentment: enjoy what comes honestly and stop the anxious chase after what is out of reach. For a householder it is usually applied to cravings and comparison, not to giving up work or responsibilities.
misreadings: Not a counsel of laziness or of abandoning needed effort; it is an ascetic's vow, and even he accepts only what is lawful (dharmya).
Not a claim that whatever happens is fine; the surrounding speech is about inner equanimity, not about tolerating harm.
cautions: The surrounding speech is close to fatalism: the sage says everything comes by its own nature or destiny, and Ganguli's note glosses him as not grieving even at a son's death. Avoid pairing it with fresh grief.
For a reader in poverty or job loss, 'don't chase what is hard to get' can sound dismissive.
speaks_to: fatigue from chasing promotions, money or status
wanting to enjoy what one already has
simplifying life after a period of striving
not_for: someone who needs to pursue medical care, a job or justice and is being told to stop trying
low mood with loss of motivation, where 'don't chase' could deepen withdrawal
fresh bereavement

attribution_note: Indra, in the form of a jackal, speaks to Kashyapa, a young brahmin (a rishi's son); Bhishma narrates the story to Yudhishthira to show that wisdom is a person's refuge. The man who knocked Kashyapa down was a proud, prosperous vaishya driving his chariot carelessly.
translation_note: Accurate. The line changes 'we' to 'I', which is fine; the jackal speaks for creatures without hands.
context: A prosperous merchant carelessly runs down the young ascetic Kashyapa with his chariot; humiliated and in pain, Kashyapa decides a poor man has no use for life and resolves to die. Indra appears as a jackal and points out what he already has: a human body, hands, learning. The jackal cannot pull out a thorn or brush off biting insects. He goes on to say craving grows like fire fed with fuel, and that he refuses suicide himself. Kashyapa then recognises Indra and returns home.

key_terms.sense: longing for (the state of) those who have hands

core_teaching: What one already has, a human body with working hands, is a greater gain than the money one is grieving for; despair over wealth forgets this. The jackal's wider point is that craving is never satisfied, so contentment, not more gain, ends sorrow.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders the jackal as listing what hands make possible: removing thorns and insects, building shelter, clothing, food. His note on the thirst image says even copious drinking only slakes thirst for a while before it returns.
The critical text (12.173.11-12) has the jackal exclaim how fully those with hands achieve their aims: creatures like him long for hands as Kashyapa longs for wealth, and no gain beats having hands.

practical_reading: Used as a reminder to count basic capacities (a working body, hands, the chance to act) when a setback or humiliation makes life feel worthless.
misreadings: Not an argument that a person in despair should simply feel grateful and get over it; in the story the jackal also stays to talk Kashyapa through it.
The ranking of births (jackal below human, brahmin above others) is the jackal's worldview, not a teaching to pass on.
cautions: The story is about a man resolving to end his life. Do not serve this verse as a response to suicidal thoughts; such a reader needs crisis support, not a parable.
The jackal's speech includes caste and rebirth hierarchy (he says he was reborn a jackal for being a sceptic) which can alienate modern readers.
Gratitude-for-hands framing can hurt readers with limb loss or disability.
speaks_to: feeling worthless after a humiliation or financial setback
forgetting ordinary blessings in a bad week
not_for: anyone expressing suicidal thoughts or self-harm
readers with disability or limb loss
acute grief

lord of past, future and present

core_teaching: A prayer of surrender: the devotee takes refuge in the Lord who governs all time. In context it is meant to be kept in mind daily and especially at the moment of death.

misreadings: Not a promise that taking refuge will change outward events.
cautions: In context this is a deathbed recitation; keep that framing away from readers who are suicidal or fear dying.

attribution_note: Bali (Vali), son of Virochana, to Indra (Shakra); narrated by Bhishma to Yudhishthira, who had asked how a king crushed by time should live.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Katthitum' is to boast or brag.
context: Indra, having defeated the asuras, asks Brahma where his old rival Bali is; Brahma says he lives as an ass (or camel, bull or horse) in an empty house, and forbids Indra to kill him, telling him to ask Bali for instruction instead. Indra rides up on Airavata and taunts Bali with his lost splendour. Bali first says his treasures lie hidden and will reappear when his time returns, then delivers this rebuke; he adds that the wise neither grieve in misery nor exult in prosperity.

key_terms.sense: one whose fortunes are full / one who has lost them

core_teaching: Mocking a fallen rival does not fit the dignity of the one on top. Bali answers contempt without self-pity, pointing to the boaster's lack of wisdom.

commentaries.gist: In Ganguli's rendering Bali says such taunting is unworthy of Indra's name and lineage, that the wise feel neither grief in misery nor glee in good times, and that Indra will talk differently once he falls too.
The critical text (12.216.26) gives the same rebuke: boasting at one who has lost everything, while oneself prospering, befits neither Indra's fame nor his lineage.

practical_reading: Applied to winners who gloat and to people being mocked after a fall: dignity lies in not answering contempt with self-pity, and success does not entitle anyone to look down on others.
misreadings: Not a claim that the fallen person must stay silent about mistreatment.
cautions: Bali is in a degraded animal birth; the story uses rebirth imagery that some readers may find strange.
speaks_to: being mocked or pitied after a fall
not_for: situations of ongoing bullying or abuse, where the reader needs protection rather than composure
research_note: No classical commentary found; the second note is the critical-text translation, not a commentary.

attribution_note: Bali to Indra, narrated by Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Broadly accurate, but 'time ripens everything' softens 'kālaḥ pacati': Ganguli notes the literal sense is 'Time cooks everything', which includes consuming and bringing to an end, not only maturing. Consider 'time ripens and wears down everything'.
context: In the second chapter of the dialogue Indra taunts Bali again. Bali answers at length that Time, not anyone's own deeds, gives and takes away; he says that if Time had not turned against him he could strike Indra down with his fist even now, but this is not the time for valour. He goes on to say thousands of Indras have passed and Indra too will pass.

key_terms.sense: a time for valour, for putting forth strength
a time for peace / for forbearance (BORI)

core_teaching: Bali reads his situation as a season set by Time: strength is not lost but held back, because this is a time for forbearance. Time establishes things and also brings them to their end, so the present turn will also change.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as: this is not the time for prowess but for peace and tranquillity; Time establishes all things and leads them to their final consummation. His footnote says the literal phrase is 'Time cooks everything'.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha, as reported in Ganguli's note on the same speech
commentaries.gist: On Bali's claim that the slayer is not the doer, Nilakantha (via Ganguli) glosses 'slain' as the lifeless body: whoever thinks himself the agent is the deluded one. Ganguli links this to Bhagavad Gita 2.19.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to strategic patience: in some seasons the wise choice is to hold back, conserve strength and wait, knowing circumstances will turn.
misreadings: Not resignation to injustice: Bali says he could fight and chooses not to because the time is wrong.
Not proof that nothing one does matters; the next chapter (Shri's speech) adds that Bali's own lapses in conduct are why fortune left him.
cautions: Bali's doctrine that Time, not people, is the doer can feel dismissive to someone harmed by a specific person.
Mentions being 'swept away by Time'; mild mortality theme.
speaks_to: a setback where pushing harder would backfire
waiting out a hard season at work
not_for: someone in an abusive or unsafe situation who needs to act now
someone told to 'wait' when urgent help is needed

attribution_note: Bali to Indra, narrated by Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Lolā' (fickle, restless) describes Shri, Fortune personified as a goddess; the line's 'success' is a fair modern equivalent.
context: Near the end of his long reply on Time, Bali tells Indra that many thousands of Indras, greater than he, have passed away and Indra will too. Royal Fortune, which Indra thinks is his to keep, lived in them and in Bali before moving on; Bali tells Indra to stop boasting and be calm, since she will leave him quickly too. In the next chapter Shri herself steps out of Bali's body and explains to Indra why she left him.

key_terms.sense: royal fortune, the goddess of sovereignty and prosperity
does not stay in one place

core_teaching: Success and power are not possessions: fortune has moved through countless holders and will move on, so pride in it is a mistake. Bali says it calmly, which is itself the lesson.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders Fortune as unsubstantial and unreal, never dwelling long in one place, having lived in thousands of Indras superior to Indra, and warns that, seeing his vanity, she will soon desert him too.

commentaries.who: Sequel in the text: Shri's own explanation (Ganguli section CCXXV)
commentaries.gist: Shri says Time moves her, yet adds she dwells in truth, gifts, vows, austerity, prowess and virtue; Bali lost these and grew boastful, so she left. She then divides herself among earth, waters, fire and the good.

practical_reading: Used to keep success in perspective: a title, a market position or a winning streak has been held by many before and will pass to others, so hold it lightly and do not look down on those who lost it.
misreadings: Not a claim that effort and conduct are irrelevant; the sequel ties fortune to virtues like truthfulness and generosity.
cautions: The sequel says fortune left Bali because of his faults; a reader who has lost a job or business could hear blame. Keep the focus on impermanence, not fault.
For someone at the bottom, 'it will move on' may sound like empty comfort.
speaks_to: staying humble after a win or promotion
envy of someone who now has what you lost
founders or leaders anxious to hold on to success

attribution_note: Tuladhara, a trader of Varanasi, to the ascetic Jajali; narrated by Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Jajali performed such severe austerities that birds nested and raised their young in his matted hair, and he grew proud of his merit. A voice from the sky said he was not the equal of Tuladhara, a merchant of Varanasi. Jajali went to him; Tuladhara already knew his story. Asked where a trader got such wisdom, Tuladhara says dharma is the ancient way of friendliness and doing good to all; he buys and sells without cheating, harms no one, keeps his scales even toward all beings, and then states this definition.

key_terms.sense: delighting in the welfare of all

core_teaching: The one who truly knows dharma is not the great ascetic but the person who is a constant friend to all and works for everyone's good in action, thought and speech. Ordinary honest life, lived without harm, can carry the highest goodness.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Tuladhara buys and sells without cheating, harms no creature or as little as necessity allows, and says his scales are even toward all: he weighs every being as equal, neither praising nor blaming others.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha, as reported in Ganguli's notes
commentaries.gist: The commentator notes that the second line spells out what this 'eternal dharma with its mysteries' consists of: universal friendliness and doing good. Ganguli's note on the scales says Tuladhara counts a Brahmana no heavier than a Chandala.

practical_reading: Teachers use Tuladhara to say goodness is available in ordinary work: deal fairly, wish everyone well, and let thought, word and action match. Spiritual pride in one's practice is the trap Jajali fell into.
misreadings: Not a claim that austerity or practice is worthless; the point is that pride in it is.
'Friend to all' does not mean having no boundaries with people who harm you.
cautions: The chapter goes on into criticism of animal sacrifice and farming as cruel; some readers may find it preachy if they read on.
speaks_to: people who feel their ordinary job is spiritually second-rate
wanting a simple test of a good life
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship who might hear 'be a friend to all' as 'keep accommodating'

attribution_note: Chirakari reasoning with himself; within Bhishma's narration to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit reads 'puruṣaṃ' and the translation follows it ('a grown person is freed from his bonds'). That word is a corruption: the digital Kumbakonam text has the garbled 'puraṣpaṃ', the BORI text reads 'puṣpaṃ' (flower), and Ganguli translates 'flower'. Correct sense: 'A flower is loosed from its stalk, a fruit falls from the tree; but a father, however troubled by love for his son, never lets go of him' (BORI: never lets go of his affection). context: Yudhishthira asks whether a hard, painful duty should be done quickly or after long thought. Bhishma tells of Chirakari ('the one who acts slowly'), son of the sage Gautama, mocked as lazy for weighing everything. Suspecting his wife (Ahalya) of infidelity, Gautama orders Chirakari to kill his mother and leaves for the forest. Chirakari agrees, then deliberates at length on what is owed to a father and to a mother. This verse closes his reflection on the father: the father is dharma, heaven and the highest austerity, and unlike a flower or fruit that drops away, he never releases his child. He then turns to think about his mother.
core_teaching: Flowers and fruit detach naturally, but a father's bond with his child does not, even when that love costs him pain. Chirakari uses this to weigh the father's claim before weighing the mother's.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as the flower falling from its stalk and the fruit from its tree, while the father, whatever his distress, never abandons the son; Chirakari then sets out to think about the mother.

commentaries.gist: The notes name the mother as Ahalya and, on Gautama's later speech, say the wrong arose from Indra's lust and Ahalya committed no transgression.

practical_reading: Read as a tribute to a parent's steady love, the kind that holds on through a child's mistakes and the parent's own pain.
misreadings: Not a statement that adult children never become independent.

cautions: The surrounding story is a father ordering his son to kill his mother over suspected infidelity; Indra had seduced her in disguise. Domestic violence and sexual deception themes.

context: Narada, visiting the young Shuka (Vyasa's son, who is set on liberation), offers to teach him what is for his highest good, and passes on what the sage Sanatkumara once told a gathering of rishis about knowledge, renunciation, restraint and truth. Just before, Sanatkumara says there is nothing higher than truth; this verse then refines what counts as truth.

key_terms.sense: what I hold to be truth

core_teaching: Truthful speech is good, but the measure of truth is finally the welfare of beings: what is truly for the good of all is what deserves the name of truth.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli warns the line is often misread: it does not license sacrificing truth for convenience, only covers rare cases where a fact would cause real harm, such as betraying hiding travellers to robbers.
Manu: speak what is true and pleasant; never a pleasant falsehood. Medhatithi adds that where a truth would only wound, one may stay silent, but must not speak a comforting lie.

commentaries.who: Parallel in the hunter's teaching (Vana Parva, BORI 3.203.42)
commentaries.gist: The same idea recurs in the Vana Parva: telling the truth is the better course, and what most fully benefits creatures is regarded as the highest truth.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to hard conversations: tell the truth, but choose which true words to say, when and how, so that they help rather than merely discharge.
misreadings: Not a licence for white lies or convenient untruth (Ganguli explicitly rejects this).
Not a reason to withhold truths someone needs, such as a diagnosis or a safety risk.
cautions: Readers recovering from being lied to 'for their own good' may find the verse uncomfortable; frame it as choosing helpful truths, not replacing truth.
speaks_to: people who use 'just being honest' as cover for cruelty
parents deciding what to tell children
not_for: someone deciding whether to conceal wrongdoing; it should not read as permission to deceive
research_note: An Indology list post (S. Vidyasankar, 1995) notes the verse is easily read as making benefit the test of truth; that utilitarian edge is exactly what Ganguli's footnote guards against.

core_teaching: Destiny and effort are not rivals: destiny is the seed, effort the field, and nothing grows without both; but since effort is the part in one's hands, it is the decisive one.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli: as tilled soil left unsown yields nothing, so destiny avails nothing without exertion; one's acts are the soil and destiny, the accumulated acts of past births, is the seed.

misreadings: Not 'everything is up to you'; the verse keeps a real role for what one is given.

cautions: A reader blaming themselves for an outcome outside their control (illness, layoffs) could hear 'you didn't try enough'.

not_for: grief over a loss nobody could have prevented

core_teaching: Age wears down every faculty, yet craving does not age with it; desire outlives the very senses that serve it.

commentaries.gist: Telang's version: restraining avarice by courage, one should wish for sovereignty in the self; this is sovereignty and there is no other, for the self properly understood is the sovereign.

practical_reading: Used as a reframe of ambition: the hardest and most worthwhile conquest is over one's own greed and cravings.
misreadings: Not a rejection of worldly responsibility; Ambarisha remained a king.
speaks_to: impulse spending and greed at work
not_for: someone in financial distress, where 'greed' framing misfires

attribution_note: Arjuna to Krishna on the chariot, on the way back to Hastinapura after the Anugita (the Kumbakonam chapter heading places the praise midway on the road). Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. The bracketed sentence ('Protect us, your devotees who rely on you, here and hereafter') is a southern insertion absent from BORI and Ganguli; our translation rightly brackets it.
context: After the Anugita, Krishna has Daruka yoke the chariot and they set out for Hastinapura. On the way Arjuna thanks him: through Krishna's grace the king has won, enemies are slain, and the Pandavas, with him as protector, crossed the Kuru ocean using him as their raft. He then praises Krishna as the soul of the universe.

key_terms.sense: the ocean of the Kurus (the war)

core_teaching: Arjuna gratefully acknowledges that the Pandavas survived the war only because Krishna was their protector, the raft on which they crossed.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli: through Krishna the Pandavas have a powerful protector; having obtained him for their raft, they have crossed the Kuru ocean. Arjuna then salutes him as soul and maker of the universe.
The critical text has the two-line verse only; the extra line asking protection 'here and hereafter' is not there.

practical_reading: Used for gratitude after coming through a hard period: naming who or what carried you across.
misreadings: Not a claim that the war or its suffering was good.
cautions: The 'ocean' is a war in which countless people died; keep the gratitude framing, not triumph.
speaks_to: gratitude after recovering from illness or crisis
not_for: someone who did not come through (bereaved by the same crisis)

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 14.66.15 = BORI 14.65.15 = Ganguli, Asvamedha Parva section LXVI.
attribution_note: Kunti to Krishna, with Draupadi, Subhadra and the other women weeping behind her. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Suprajā Devakī tvayā': through you Devaki is blessed in her child (Ganguli: regarded as an excellent mother).
context: Krishna returns to Hastinapura for the horse sacrifice. Uttara's son is born dead, struck in the womb by Ashvatthama's weapon. Kunti rushes to Krishna, praises him, and reminds him of his vow to revive the child. Krishna, by the power of his truthfulness, brings the infant back to life, and he is named Parikshit.
core_teaching: In the family's darkest moment Kunti declares Krishna their only refuge and foundation; the whole line now depends on him.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli: choked with tears, Kunti tells Krishna that Devaki is honoured for bearing him, that he is their refuge and glory, and that the race depends on him; she asks him to revive the child as he vowed.
The Bhagavata places Kunti's famous prayers right after Krishna shields Uttara's unborn child: she recalls every danger he saved them from and says the Pandavas have no other protector.

practical_reading: Used as a prayer of total dependence in crisis, when all human resources have run out.
misreadings: Not a promise that prayer will reverse a death (our misuse note is right).
cautions: The scene is a stillbirth. Keep this card away from pregnancy loss, stillbirth, infant loss and infertility, as our note says.
Even outside those contexts, the story's miracle can make readers whose loved ones were not saved feel abandoned.
speaks_to: family emergencies where one turns to prayer
devotional readers seeking words of refuge
not_for: pregnancy loss, stillbirth, infant or child loss
bereavement after a loved one was not saved

attribution_note: Dharma, disguised as the guest, to the gleaner brahmin; within the mongoose's tale told to the assembled priests at Yudhishthira's sacrifice. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Our line ('Be gentle with yourself and others when money is tight') is a modern application, not in the verse; in context Dharma is praising the gleaner for overcoming hunger, not excusing lapses.
context: At the close of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice a mongoose, half its body golden, declares the great rite worth less than a poor gleaner's gift. During a famine in Kurukshetra a brahmin living by gleaning, with his wife, son and daughter-in-law, had at last gathered a little barley flour when a hungry guest arrived; each gave his own share. The guest revealed himself as Dharma and praised the gift; the mongoose, rolling in the spilt flour, turned half gold. Dharma speaks this as he praises the gift: because hunger destroys judgement and steadiness, the one who conquers hunger to give conquers heaven.
core_teaching: Hunger drives out judgement, a sense of right and steadiness; that is why giving while starving is so great a feat.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli: hunger destroys wisdom and drives off righteous understanding, and one overwhelmed by it casts off fortitude; therefore one who conquers hunger conquers heaven.

commentaries.who: Devdutt Pattanaik on the half-golden mongoose
commentaries.gist: Pattanaik reads the tale as measuring generosity by what it costs the giver: the poor man gave his last meal, feeling another's hunger while rising above his own.

practical_reading: Read today as both admiration for those who give in hardship and realism about what deprivation does to anyone's choices.
misreadings: Not a claim that poor people are less moral.
Not a demand that people in need give away what they have.
cautions: Readers facing food insecurity may feel judged; use the compassionate reading.
not_for: eating disorders or fasting contexts
readers in acute food insecurity, if framed as moral test

attribution_note: Dharma, disguised as the guest, to the gleaner brahmin; within the mongoose's tale told to the assembled priests at Yudhishthira's sacrifice. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. The next verse gives King Rantideva, who gave only water when he had nothing and reached heaven.
context: At the close of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice a mongoose, half its body golden, declares the great rite worth less than a poor gleaner's gift. Dharma says heaven's door is seen by those who give according to their ability, then states this rule of proportion.

key_terms.sense: one who has (the means of) a thousand

core_teaching: Giving is measured by proportion to one's means: a hundred from a thousand, ten from a hundred, and a little water from one who has nothing, all bear equal merit.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one who gives a hundred having a thousand, ten having a hundred, or a handful of water having nothing, all earn equal merit; Rantideva, stripped of wealth, reached heaven by a little water given with a pure heart.

commentaries.who: Devdutt Pattanaik on the half-golden mongoose
commentaries.gist: Pattanaik: the king's ritual charity was vast in wealth but small in proportion to what he had, while the beggar's last meal was everything; generosity is measured by its cost to the giver.

practical_reading: Encourages people with little to give without embarrassment, and people with much to measure their giving honestly against their means.
misreadings: Not a claim that large donations are worthless.
speaks_to: people who feel their small contribution doesn't count
students and young earners starting to give
not_for: someone pressured to give beyond their means

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 14.92.77 = BORI 14.93.73 = Ganguli, Asvamedha Parva section XC.
attribution_note: Dharma, disguised as the guest, to the gleaner brahmin; within the mongoose's tale told to the assembled priests at Yudhishthira's sacrifice. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Our Sanskrit has 'śruddhāpūtaiḥ', a typo for 'śraddhāpūtaiḥ' (purified by faith).
context: At the close of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice a mongoose, half its body golden, declares the great rite worth less than a poor gleaner's gift. During a famine in Kurukshetra a brahmin living by gleaning, with his wife, son and daughter-in-law, had at last gathered a little barley flour when a hungry guest arrived; each gave his own share. The guest revealed himself as Dharma and praised the gift; the mongoose, rolling in the spilt flour, turned half gold. After the Rantideva example, Dharma states this principle and adds the case of King Nriga, who gave thousands of cows but fell into hell for giving one that was not his.
core_teaching: Dharma is pleased not by grand gifts but by small ones that were honestly earned and sincerely given.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the deity of righteousness is never gratified so much by costly gifts as by things of little value, lawfully acquired and given with devotion and faith; Nriga fell for giving one cow not his own.

commentaries.who: Pradip Bhattacharya, essay on the Ashvamedha Parva
commentaries.gist: Bhattacharya reads the mongoose episode as the epic's verdict on the great sacrifice: lavish gifts do not equal one poor man's offering to a guest who was Dharma himself, and no number of rituals makes one virtuous.

practical_reading: Used to stress the ethics of giving: clean money and a sincere heart matter more than the size or publicity of a donation.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of large-scale philanthropy.
